# Cooling the City: How Urban Design Can Tame Summer Heat

Every summer, cities become furnaces. Concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight all day and release it slowly at night, so urban temperatures routinely run five to ten degrees Fahrenheit hotter than surrounding countryside—a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. This gap is not merely a matter of comfort. Heat is among the deadliest weather hazards in modern cities, killing more Americans in a typical year than hurricanes, floods, or tornadoes, and its victims are disproportionately elderly residents, outdoor workers, and people in low-income neighborhoods. Because climate change is making heat waves longer, hotter, and more frequent, the question of how cities can make summer bearable is no longer a design nicety. It is a matter of public health and basic justice. The encouraging news is that cities have powerful tools available: trees, thoughtful street design, better housing, and expanded public transit. The harder truth is that each of these tools involves tradeoffs, and residents must weigh costs, inconveniences, and competing values as their neighborhoods change.
